title: Three Big Areas for Development in Most Settings
author: Sherrington, Tom
summary: Drawing on observations from hundreds of school visits, Tom Sherrington identifies three recurring areas where most schools need deep, sustained work: inclusive teaching (systematically engaging every learner, not just volunteers), responsive teaching (taking formative action in real time based on evidence gathered during the lesson), and teaching through talk (developing oracy as a central vehicle for learning, not a peripheral add-on). Sherrington argues these three are really one agenda from different angles: all converge on ensuring 100% of learners are actively involved in thinking, that teachers interact with student progress in meaningful ways, and that teachers respond in ways that deepen learning rather than just delivering content. The inclusive teaching strand targets the entrenched default of 'can anyone tell me?'—which systematically excludes the students who most need engagement. The responsive teaching strand centers on Formative Action: gathering real-time evidence and actually doing something with it rather than proceeding linearly as though all students succeed in unison. The oracy strand, influenced by Voice 21, positions student talk as load-bearing for both inclusion and responsive teaching, not an extra thing on the outside but the practice at the center.
points: The entrenched default of seeking volunteers and accepting one answer from one student is 'utterly ludicrously inadequate'—the whole point of classroom interaction is that every student is able to succeed, which requires finding out how all students are doing in real time.

Responsive teaching centers on formative action: teachers must gather responses during lesson flow, interpret the evidence, and actually do something about gaps, errors, and misconceptions—not just proceed linearly assuming success.

Adaptive teaching requires agile lesson design that is ready to branch rather than only move forward, as schemes of work built to go one direction in unison fail the learners for whom instruction most needs to adapt.

Oracy is not peripheral to the teaching agenda—it directly enables both inclusion (every voice is valued) and responsiveness (teachers hear what students think and respond); the three big areas are arguably one integrated agenda.
Students who find learning hard matter as much as students who fly through; they are not an inconvenience—their learning needs are the learning needs the profession is called to serve.
quotes: We need to do some pretty serious work to reverse the default of ‘can anyone tell me’ to become ‘is there anyone here who isn’t sure?
I think this issue needs extensive exploration in many settings because true, systematic inclusion just isn’t the norm - yet!

The key concept lies in the word Action: teachers (and students themselves) need to evaluate success using responses that are generated during a lesson flow, interpret that information and do something about it! If you have used show-me boards and find a number of learners have gaps, errors or misconception, you need to take action!
Adaptive teaching and formative action require a much more agile approach and this needs some deep work so that teachers are ready for it and deploying the approach day in day out.
Students who find learning hard matter as much as those who fly through; they are not an inconvenience - the learning process they need is the learning process that is needed!

it’s increasingly clear to me that the oracy agenda can and should play a massive role in deepening learning. Oracy is not some extra thing on the outside; another thing to do. It’s right at the centre.
We learn through talk. Oracy supports the inclusion agenda: We value every voice. And combing these together, oracy supports the responsiveness agenda - we listen, engage and respond.
